The software development kits (SDKs) that applications used to validate tokens were not updated to tell the two kinds apart, so some applications, mail among them, accepted a token signed by *any* listed key. A consumer key could open enterprise mailboxes.

blocks.title: How a consumer key opened enterprise mail

scenes.caption: Intended design: consumer keys sign consumer tokens and enterprise keys sign enterprise tokens. The 2016 consumer key should have been retired in 2021.
The actor obtains the 2016 key. The CSRB found Microsoft still could not say how; the key was still active and still listed.
With the private key the actor signs tokens for chosen victims. Cryptographically they are perfect: the signature is genuine.
The flaw: validation trusted every key on the mixed list, never asking whether this key belonged to the enterprise issuer. A consumer-signed token passed.
Mailboxes opened, from 15 May 2023. Every read still produced audit events, which is how the State Department noticed on 15 June.

blocks.md:
**Detection.** The US State Department's security operations centre (SOC) spotted anomalies on 15 June 2023 and the next day saw alerts from a custom rule it called "Big Yellow Taxi", built on the **MailItemsAccessed** log, which records access to mailbox items. CISA's advisory gives the signal: MailItemsAccessed events with an **AppId** (application identifier) that did not normally access mailboxes in that environment. That log needed Microsoft's premium audit tier (E5 or G5 licences at the time), which, the CSRB notes, many victims did not have.

Microsoft had invalidated the stolen key on 24 June. On 26 June it realised the tokens were signed by a consumer key that should not have been signing at all, and by 27 June it had cleared caches so credentials derived from the key stopped working. It almost at once saw the actor switch to phishing. After the key was dead, any attempt to use it was itself a high-confidence detection.

Shir Tamari of Wiz, a cloud security company, reported in July 2023 that the acquired key's certificate was issued on 5 April 2016 and expired on 4 April 2021, yet the key was still trusted. Tamari argued that, under certain conditions, it could also have signed tokens for other applications that validate against Microsoft's common or consumer key lists, not only Outlook.

The CSRB found that the intrusion was preventable and should never have occurred, and that Microsoft's security culture was inadequate and required an overhaul. Its review is the best single primary source on the case.

blocks.code:
from datetime import date
import jwt  # PyJWT

# One trusted issuer, one key set. A key is only good for the issuer it came from.
ISSUER = "https://login.example.com/enterprise"
AUDIENCE = "https://mail.example.com"
enterprise_keys = jwt.PyJWKClient(ISSUER + "/keys")   # NOT a mixed "common" list

def verify_mail_token(token: str) -> dict:
    key = enterprise_keys.get_signing_key_from_jwt(token).key
    return jwt.decode(token, key, algorithms=["RS256"],
                      issuer=ISSUER, audience=AUDIENCE,
                      options={"require": ["exp", "iss", "aud", "sub"]})

# Key hygiene: alert on any signing key still active past its rotation date
MAX_AGE_DAYS = 365
active_keys = [{"kid": "consumer-2016", "created": date(2016, 4, 5)},
               {"kid": "ent-2023-03", "created": date(2023, 3, 1)}]
today = date(2023, 6, 1)
for k in active_keys:
    age = (today - k["created"]).days
    if age > MAX_AGE_DAYS:
        print(f"ALERT {k['kid']} active for {age} days: rotate and revoke")
# ALERT consumer-2016 active for 2613 days: rotate and revoke
blocks.caption: The two lessons in code: keys fetched only from our own issuer, never a mixed list, with iss and aud checked; and an alert on any signing key active past its rotation date. Tested: a key outside the enterprise set fails the signature; a consumer issuer fails the iss check.

blocks.md: A valid signature is only as good as the question "is this key one that this issuer uses for this kind of token?" RFC 8725 says it plainly: check that the keys belong to the issuer. And signing keys are crown jewels: rotate them, retire them, alert on their age, and log every use.

What to log for your own tokens: the kid and iss of every accepted token, and the client or app id. A token signed by a retired kid, or an app id that never touched a resource before, are exactly the two signals that exposed Storm-0558.

blocks.question: Storm-0558's forged tokens carried genuine signatures. Which check, done correctly, would have rejected them at Exchange Online?
options: Checking the token was not expired
Checking that the signing key belonged to the enterprise issuer the service trusts, instead of accepting any key on a mixed list
Checking that the token was base64url encoded
Checking the user's password
blocks.explain: The signature was valid for the consumer key, and the token was presented within its lifetime. The missing question was whether that key had any authority over enterprise mail. Binding keys to issuers (RFC 8725, section 3.8) is that question.

blocks.question: How did the first victim detect the intrusion?
options: Microsoft's antivirus flagged the actor
A user reported a phishing email
A custom alert on the MailItemsAccessed audit log showed mailbox access by an application that did not normally access mail
The forged tokens failed signature checks and caused errors
blocks.explain: The tokens worked perfectly, so there were no errors. The State Department's alert on an unusual AppId in MailItemsAccessed events was the signal, which CISA then described for other agencies in AA23-193A.

lessons.title: Storing tokens in browsers, short lifetimes and revocation

blocks.md: A token is only as safe as the place it is kept. For browser apps the threat that matters most is **malicious JavaScript running in your page**, from cross-site scripting (XSS, from the web security model course) or a compromised third-party script. RFC 10017, *OAuth 2.0 for Browser-Based Applications* (an IETF Best Current Practice published in August 2026), works through what such code can do. Its key observation: injected code can read tokens from storage, and it can also just ask for new tokens or send requests through the user's browser, exactly as your own code would.

blocks.title: Where a browser app can keep tokens (1 = yes)

scenes.caption: Rows are storage options, columns are properties. RFC 10017 describes each one; red-ish cells are not all bad, they are tradeoffs.
localStorage and sessionStorage: any script on the origin can read them. RFC 10017: they do not protect against malicious JavaScript. sessionStorage is per tab, slightly less exposed.
Memory only (a variable or closure): gone on reload. RFC 10017 notes closures are hard to secure because injected code can replace the functions they call.
A cookie written by JavaScript is the worst of both: readable by script and also sent automatically. RFC 10017 says this practice is NOT RECOMMENDED.
Backend for Frontend: tokens never reach the browser. It holds only a Secure, HttpOnly cookie for the BFF, so script cannot read it, but you need CSRF defences.

blocks.md:
RFC 10017 presents three architectures in decreasing order of security:

1. **Backend for Frontend (BFF)**: a small server of your own is the OAuth client (a confidential one), keeps all tokens server-side, and gives the browser only a session cookie that it must mark `Secure` and `HttpOnly`, and should mark `SameSite=Strict`. The browser calls the BFF, which adds the access token and forwards to the API. Injected script can still make requests through the user's browser while the page is open, but it cannot steal tokens to use elsewhere.
2. **Token-mediating backend**: a backend gets tokens but hands access tokens to the browser.
3. **Browser-based OAuth client**: everything in JavaScript, with PKCE and in-memory or worker-isolated storage.

**Short lifetimes and revocation.** A self-contained access token cannot be recalled; it is valid until `exp`. RFC 6750 suggests bearer tokens of an hour or less. The shorter the lifetime, the shorter a thief's window, and the refresh token, which the authorization server *can* revoke, becomes the long-term control.

RFC 7009 defines a **revocation endpoint**: a client posts a token there (for example at logout) and the server invalidates it. For refresh tokens and opaque tokens that is immediate. For JWT access tokens it only helps if APIs check something, such as introspection or a small denylist of revoked token ids (`jti`) kept until those tokens would have expired.

blocks.title: A stolen access token versus its lifetime

scenes.caption: 60-minute JWT access token issued at minute 0. Malware steals it at minute 10.
At minute 20 the theft is noticed and the refresh token is revoked. The attacker's copy of the JWT still works: nothing checks a revocation list.
Same story with 5-minute access tokens refreshed as needed. The stolen one dies at minute 15; after the revoke at 20 no new ones can be minted.

blocks.caption: When a JWT must die early: a denylist of revoked jti values, pruned as tokens expire. With short lifetimes it stays tiny. Tested output: True, False, then False 0 once the token would have expired anyway.

blocks.md:
**Case: Facebook "View As", September 2018.** View As let you see your own profile as another person would. Facebook's engineers explained that three bugs combined: View As wrongly showed a video upload option in the birthday-post composer; a video uploader introduced in July 2017 wrongly generated an access token with the permissions of the Facebook mobile app; and inside View As it generated that token for the person being looked up, not the viewer. The token ended up in the page's HTML, where attackers read it.

Starting from accounts they controlled, the attackers moved friend to friend in an automated way, collecting tokens for about 400,000 people and then, using their friend lists, about 30 million. Facebook saw an unusual spike of activity from 14 September, identified the attack on 25 September, and fixed it within two days.

**The response was revocation at scale.** Facebook reset the access tokens of almost 50 million accounts it believed affected, plus another 40 million that had been subject to a View As look-up in the past year, as a precaution. About 90 million people had to log in again, both to Facebook and to apps using Facebook Login, and View As was switched off. In December 2024 Ireland's Data Protection Commission fined Meta (Facebook's parent company, renamed from Facebook in 2021) EUR 251 million over the breach, which it says affected about 29 million accounts.

The lessons for token design: a feature that *mints* tokens is security-critical code; a token should carry only the permissions its purpose needs; tokens never belong in page HTML; and you need the ability to revoke tokens in bulk, by user and by time window, before you need it.

Misconception: "HttpOnly cookies make XSS harmless." They stop script from stealing the cookie, but injected script can still send requests through the user's browser while the page is open. Storage choices limit theft; only preventing XSS stops abuse.

blocks.question: Your single-page app (SPA) keeps its access and refresh tokens in localStorage. An XSS bug is found. What should you assume?
options: Nothing leaked, since localStorage is per origin
Only the access token leaked
Both tokens may have been read and sent elsewhere; revoke the refresh tokens, fix the XSS, and consider moving to a BFF
Only users on old browsers are affected
blocks.explain: Same-origin script can read localStorage in full. The refresh token is the valuable one, since it mints new access tokens; revoke them (all, if you cannot scope the exposure) and fix the injection.

blocks.question: Why do short access token lifetimes matter more for JWTs than for opaque tokens?
options: JWTs are larger
A JWT is usually checked locally without asking the issuer, so revocation does not reach it; only exp ends it
Opaque tokens cannot expire
JWTs cannot carry exp
blocks.explain: An opaque token is looked up on use, so deleting it works at once. A locally verified JWT has no such lookup unless you add a denylist or introspection, so its lifetime is the exposure window.

lessons.title: GraphQL risks: introspection, batching and query depth

blocks.md:
GraphQL moves query design from the server to the client. That is convenient and also means the client decides how much work each request costs. Four GraphQL-specific risks follow, each of which maps onto the API Top 10.

**Introspection.** GraphQL can describe itself: querying the `__schema` field returns every type, field and argument. graphql.org notes that for APIs used only by your own apps it is typically not needed in production, and that disabling it there is common to reduce attack surface. It is not a security boundary, though: hiding the schema does not secure the fields in it.

**Batching and aliases.** One HTTP request can carry many operations: an array of queries, or one query that asks for the same field many times under different **aliases** (names the client gives to each copy of a field). OWASP's API2 example uses this to send hundreds of login guesses in one HTTP request, sailing past a limit of three requests per minute. Rate limits must count operations and expensive fields, not HTTP requests.

**Depth and amount.** Types often link back to each other (a user has friends, who are users with friends). OWASP's GraphQL Cheat Sheet notes that both nesting depth and the requested amount (`first: 99999999`) are unlimited by default, which can lead to denial of service.

blocks.title: Objects a nested friends query can request

scenes.caption: Each level asks for friends(first: 100) of every user above it, so the count multiplies: 100, 10,000, 1,000,000 by depth 3.
At depth 6 one small query asks for 10^12 objects. One HTTP request, one line of text.
Capping page size helps but does not save you: with first: 10 depth 6 is still a million. You need depth and cost limits together.

blocks.code:
from graphql import parse   # graphql-core, the Python port of graphql-js

MAX_DEPTH = 5

def depth(node, level=0):
    sel = getattr(node, "selection_set", None)
    if sel is None:
        return level
    return max(depth(child, level + 1) for child in sel.selections)

def check(query: str):
    d = max(depth(op) for op in parse(query).definitions)
    return f"reject: depth {d} > {MAX_DEPTH}" if d > MAX_DEPTH else f"ok: depth {d}"

print(check("{ me { name orders(first: 10) { id total } } }"))
print(check("""{ user(id: 1) { friends(first: 100) { friends(first: 100) {
               friends(first: 100) { friends(first: 100) { friends(first: 100)
               { name } } } } } } }"""))
# ok: depth 3
# reject: depth 7 > 5
# Simplified: real limiters also expand fragments and count aliases and list
# sizes (cost analysis), and run before any resolver executes.
blocks.caption: A depth limit using graphql-core (the Python port of the reference GraphQL implementation) to parse the query before any resolver runs. Tested: a normal query has depth 3; the nested friends query has depth 7 and is rejected.

blocks.md:
**Authorization in every resolver.** A **resolver** is the function that fetches one field. Because a client can reach the same object through many paths (`order.customer`, `user(id:)`, `search`), checking permissions only on the top-level query is not enough. Check per object and per field in the resolver or a shared data layer, the BOLA and property-level lessons of the access control course. Peloton's 2021 exposure, recalled from that course, included GraphQL endpoints.

**Defences, from OWASP and graphql.org:** depth and amount limits, query cost analysis, limits on aliases and batched operations, timeouts, pagination, introspection and the GraphiQL explorer (a browser-based IDE, integrated development environment, for GraphQL) off in production for private APIs, and, for first-party apps, **operation safelisting**: the server only runs queries registered in advance.

In GraphQL one request can mean one operation or thousands. Price requests by the work they ask for, check authorization where each field is resolved, and let the server, not the client, decide what is too expensive.

Defender view: log the operation name, depth, computed cost, alias count and operations per HTTP request. Alert on introspection queries in production, on batches of login or OTP mutations, and on a client whose cost per minute jumps. These fields are invisible in a plain web server log, which only sees POST /graphql.

blocks.question: Login is rate limited to 3 HTTP requests per minute. An attacker sends one POST /graphql containing 500 aliased login mutations. What went wrong?
options: Nothing; 1 request is under the limit
GraphQL is encrypted
Aliases are only for queries
The limit counts HTTP requests instead of login attempts, so batching multiplies the attacker's rate by 500
blocks.explain: This is the trick in OWASP's API2 scenario, which batches an array of login queries; aliases have the same effect. Count each login mutation (and failed attempts per account) against the limit, and cap aliases and batch size for sensitive operations.

blocks.question: Introspection is disabled in production. Is the API's data now protected?
options: Yes, attackers cannot guess field names
Yes, if GraphiQL is also off
No: it removes a convenient map, but field names leak through the app's own code and traffic; authorization and cost limits are still required
No, introspection cannot be disabled
blocks.explain: graphql.org frames disabling introspection as attack surface reduction within a broader strategy. Your client app ships its queries, so anyone can read them. Security comes from checks on every field.

lessons.title: Detecting and responding to API and token attacks

blocks.md: Token attacks rarely trip the alarms built for password attacks: a stolen or forged token produces no failed logins, and the requests look normal. Detection has to come from the token and API layer itself. The cases in this course give the signals: Storm-0558 showed up as mailbox access by an unusual app id; Facebook's as an unusual spike of activity; Salesloft Drift's as an integration user running bulk exports from Tor exit nodes.

**What to log.** At the authorization server: every token issued (client id, user, scopes, grant type, PKCE used), refresh events and reuse detections, consents granted, redirect URI and state mismatches, and revocations. At every API: for each request, the token's `iss`, `sub`, `client_id` or `azp` (authorized party, the OIDC claim naming the client a token was issued to), `kid`, `jti` and scopes; for each rejected token, the reason (bad signature, wrong audience, expired, algorithm not allowed). Never log the token itself: a logged bearer token is a stolen bearer token.

Send both to your **SIEM** (security information and event management system, which collects logs from many sources and runs detection rules).

scenes.caption: Three log sources feed one place. None of them should contain raw tokens, only ids and claims.
Forgery and confusion: tokens with alg none or HS256 on an RS256 API, unknown or retired kid values, valid tokens for another audience.
Theft and replay: refresh token reuse, one jti seen from two networks, a token suddenly used from Tor or a new country.
Consent abuse: a new app granted mail or file scopes by many users in a short time, or an integration exporting far more than usual.
Abuse by volume: 429 spikes per key, enumeration of ids, GraphQL cost jumps. Every rule ends in a response playbook.

blocks.md:
**Responding**, by incident type:

1. **Stolen user tokens**: revoke that user's refresh tokens and sessions everywhere, then check what the tokens touched. For many users, do as Facebook did: bulk-reset tokens for everyone who could have been exposed.
2. **Malicious or compromised OAuth app**: revoke its consents and tokens across the tenant, block the app, then hunt through what it read (Salesloft Drift: rotate every secret the exported data contained).
3. **Signing key exposure**: publish a new key, remove the old one from the JWKS, make sure every verifier refreshes its cache, and watch for tokens still signed with the old kid, which are now attacks by definition (Storm-0558).
4. **Leaked API key**: revoke and reissue, then search logs for its use from unexpected networks.
5. Always fix the door: the validation bug, the missing scope check, the XSS that leaked tokens.

Tokens move the security perimeter into data: who issued it, with which key, for which audience, for how long. Log those fields on every request, alert on the impossible ones, and rehearse revoking at scale.

**Practise legally.** Only test systems you own or have written permission to test. Free places built for exactly this course:

- PortSwigger Web Security Academy labs on [API testing](https://portswigger.net/web-security/api-testing), [OAuth authentication](https://portswigger.net/web-security/oauth), [JWT attacks](https://portswigger.net/web-security/jwt) and [GraphQL API vulnerabilities](https://portswigger.net/web-security/graphql).
- [OWASP crAPI](https://github.com/OWASP/crAPI) (completely ridiculous API), a deliberately vulnerable API you run locally, covering the API Top 10.
- [OWASP Juice Shop](https://owasp.org/www-project-juice-shop/), which includes JWT and API challenges.

For reference, keep [RFC 9700](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700.html) (OAuth security) and [RFC 8725](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8725.html) (JWT best practices) close.

blocks.question: Your API logs show a burst of tokens with `alg: HS256` arriving at an endpoint that only ever accepts RS256. They are all rejected. What is the right reading?
options: Someone is probing for algorithm confusion; alert, identify the source and client, and confirm every verifier pins its algorithm
Harmless noise from old clients
A clock skew problem
A sign the signing key should be made shorter
blocks.explain: Honest clients never change the algorithm. A burst like this is an attacker testing whether any verifier still trusts the header, so treat it as an attack in progress even though this endpoint held.

blocks.question: You learn that an old signing key may have leaked. Which response is complete?
options: Rotate the key and wait for tokens to expire
Revoke all user passwords
Disable logging to avoid exposing the key further
Publish a new key, remove the old one from the JWKS, force verifiers to refresh their key cache, and alert on any token still signed with the old kid
blocks.explain: Removing the key from the published set is what stops new forgeries being accepted, but cached keys must be refreshed too. Afterwards any token with the old kid is a forgery attempt and a valuable detection, as Microsoft found.
